caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Namibia's debt has risen relentlessly as diamond and uranium revenues stagnated while spending grew. From 15.9% of GDP in 2009, the series low, the ratio climbed through the 2010s to 70.2% projected for 2025, the series high, with no sustained reversal. The government borrows domestically and on South African markets; the debt is mostly in rand-linked instruments, limiting currency risk. Sustainability is still judged manageable, but the one-directional trajectory is the concern: Namibia has spent two decades converting a low-debt position into a high one without building the growth to justify it, and debt service is crowding out investment.
inflation_management: Namibia's inflation is imported from South Africa via the Namibian dollar's one-to-one peg to the rand under the Common Monetary Area. It peaked at 9.5% in 2009 and troughed at 2.2% in 2020, tracking South African price dynamics: 6.1% in 2022 during the global shock, easing to a projected 3.5% in 2025. The Bank of Namibia shadows the South African Reserve Bank, so there is no independent monetary policy; inflation management is outsourced to Pretoria. The peg has delivered reasonable stability, but it also means Namibia cannot use monetary policy to address its deep structural problems of unemployment and inequality.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis hit diamonds and uranium; debt began its long climb.
Prolonged commodity downturn and drought strained revenues; debt passed 40% of GDP.
COVID-19 pushed debt to 63.9%; the economy contracted sharply.
Shell and TotalEnergies announced major offshore oil discoveries, a potential game-changer.
President Geingob died (February 2024); Nangolo Mbumba served as interim president.
November 27, 2024: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah (SWAPO) won the presidency with about 57%, becoming Namibia's first female president; sworn in March 2025.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued slow growth with debt near 70% of GDP and inflation anchored by the rand peg. The wildcard is oil: if the 2022 discoveries reach production late this decade, revenues could transform the fiscal picture; if gas-heavy fields prove uneconomic, the debt trajectory continues. Upside is an oil boom well-managed; downside is debt distress without it. Uncertainty is moderate-to-high, hinging on geology and investment decisions outside Namibia's control.
